meaning: ‘sage of the Śākya clan’, epithet of the historical Buddha Siddhārtha Gautama, MW.

pronunciation.approximation: SHAH-kyuh-moo-nih — ś is the soft palatal 'sh'; the ā of Śākya is long.
pronunciation.note: Śākyamuni is a title, not a personal name: śākya, of the Śākya clan of Kapilavastu, + muni, "sage, silent one" (Monier-Williams) — "the sage of the Śākyas." His personal name was Siddhārtha (Pāli Siddhattha), his clan name Gautama (Pāli Gotama); the tradition itself connects Śākya with the śāka (teak) tree of the clan's founding legend. The restoration keeps the palatal ś and the long ā that the ASCII "Shakyamuni" only approximates. Tier-1 by rule.

domains.title: The Sage of the Śākyas
domains.subtitle: The Renunciation, the Awakening, and the Turning of the Wheel
domains.lead: Śākyamuni is the historical Buddha: Siddhārtha Gautama of the Śākya clan, who left a palace at twenty-nine, awoke under the Bodhi tree at thirty-five, taught for forty-five years across the Ganges plain, and died at eighty between two sāla trees — the one teacher of antiquity whose birthplace an emperor certified in stone.

cards.name: The Bodhi Tree
cards.desc: The aśvattha at Uruvelā under which the ascetic became the Buddha — Bodh Gayā to this day.

cards.name: The Wheel
cards.desc: The Dhammacakra set turning at Sarnath: the first sermon, the middle way, the four noble truths.

cards.name: The Footprints
cards.desc: Buddhapāda — the earliest art dared not show him; his footprints stood for the one who had gone.

cards.name: The Twin Sāla Trees
cards.desc: The couch between two sāla trees at Kusinārā, where the teaching ended in flowers out of season.

symbols.name: The Bodhi tree
symbols.meaning: The axis of the awakening: the tree a whole religion still calls by one name

symbols.name: The earth-touching hand
symbols.meaning: Bhūmisparśa: the gesture that called the earth to witness against Māra

symbols.name: The begging bowl
symbols.meaning: The middle way in an object: neither the palace's gold nor the ash of the fire-ascetics

mythology.lead: The life of Śākyamuni is the best-attested sacred biography of the ancient world — told in the Pāli Nikāyas, versified by Aśvaghoṣa, expanded in the Nidānakathā and the Lalitavistara, and anchored in the ground by Aśoka's own inscriptions.

myths.title: The Birth at Lumbinī
myths.text: Queen Māyā, traveling to her father's house, gave birth standing in the grove at Lumbinī, holding the branch of a sāla tree; the child took seven steps and declared this his last birth. The legends multiplied — the shower of blossoms, the two streams of water, the prophecy of the sage Asita — but the place is fixed in stone: Aśoka's pillar at Rummindei, raised in his twentieth regnal year, reads in plain Prakrit, hida budhe jāte sakyamuni — "here the Buddha Śākyamuni was born." It is the only birthplace of a world teacher certified by a contemporary emperor.

myths.title: The Four Sights and the Going Forth
myths.text: Sheltered in three palaces, the young Śākyan saw what his father had fenced out: an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — the four sights the later tradition makes the hinge of his life. In the Majjhima Nikāya's Ariyapariyesanā Sutta (MN 26) he tells it himself: he shaved his hair, put on the ochre robe, and went forth from home into homelessness while still young, in the prime of life, with his parents weeping. The great renunciation — the night ride on Kaṇṭhaka with the groom Channa — became Buddhist art's first epic scene.

myths.title: The Awakening and the First Turning
myths.text: Six years of austerities on the Nairañjanā brought him to the edge of death and the discovery of the middle way; seated under the Bodhi tree at Uruvelā he withstood Māra's assault, touched the earth as his witness, and by dawn saw the four noble truths and the chain of dependent arising. Weeks later, in the deer park at Ṛṣipatana near Benares — Sarnath — he taught the five ascetics the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (SN 56.11), the setting-in-motion of the wheel: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the eightfold path. The sermon is preserved in every Buddhist canon; the wheel he turned has not stopped.

myths.title: The Last Days at Kusinārā
myths.text: The Dīgha Nikāya's Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16) follows his last journey with a chronicler's eye: the meal offered by the smith Cunda, the sickness, the couch laid northward between twin sāla trees in the Mallas' grove at Kusinārā, which burst into blossom out of season. His last instruction was a refusal of permanence itself: "All conditioned things are of a nature to decay — strive on with diligence." The Mallas cremated him as a universal monarch, and his relics were divided into eight shares and enshrined in stupas — the beginning of Buddhist sacred architecture.

lore.syncretism: Every Buddhism is his daughter: the Theravāda of the Pāli canon, the Mahāyāna that set him among countless Buddhas yet kept his biography as the pattern of all awakening, the Vajrayāna that read his life as an already-enlightened being's demonstration. East Asia naturalized the name itself — Chinese Shìjiāmóuní, Japanese Shakamuni, Korean Seokgamoni — and Southeast Asia made his earth-touching gesture the single most common Buddha image on earth. Modern scholarship from Rhys Davids onward has treated him as history's first fully-documented founder: a reformer of the Gangetic plain whose dates, places, and words can be argued from evidence, not legend alone.
lore.culturalLegacy: A third of Asia orders its calendar by him: Vesak keeps his birth, awakening, and death in one full-moon festival; the Buddhist Era counts from his parinibbāna; India's national emblem is the lion capital of the pillar Aśoka raised at his first sermon. The English word "Buddha" is his epithet — "the Awakened" — and Śākyamuni remains the name that ties the cosmic teacher back to a clan, a grove, and a date: the sage of the Śākyas, a man of one valley whose refusal to accept decay as final became a world religion.
lore.extendedMeditation: Śākyamuni's whole authority rests on a refusal: he would not call the palace enough, and he would not call the ashes enough either. The middle way is not a compromise but a discovery — that comfort and punishment are the same evasion — and it is walked, not believed. He left no creed to sign, only a path to test and a closing sentence: everything conditioned decays; be diligent.
lore.archaeology: No sacred biography of antiquity is better grounded. Lumbinī's Rummindei pillar (Aśoka's twentieth year, c. 249 BCE) names the birthplace in words; Kapilavastu's candidate sites (Piprahwa, with its inscribed relic vase of 1898, debated but famous) anchor the clan; Bodh Gayā preserves the seat itself, marked by Aśoka's shrine and the Mahābodhi temple of later centuries; Sarnath holds the Dhāmekh stupa and the lion capital that India took as its national emblem; Kusinārā (Kushinagar) keeps the parinirvāṇa temple and the cremation stupa. The eight original relic stupas of DN 16 began the tradition that Aśoka multiplied, by the later legend, to eighty-four thousand.
